cover.headline: A better business after RBIC, but the price already pays for it
cover.lead: Bosch Ltd is Robert Bosch's 70.5%-owned Indian mobility flagship: engine management and fuel injection, the aftermarket and power tools, and since Jul-2026 Bosch Chassis Systems India (RBIC: ESP/ABS, braking, airbag electronics), bought from the parent for ₹9,069 cr. Q1FY27 revenue rose 22% and the EBITDA margin reached 14%. With RBIC pooled for the full year we forecast EPS of ₹1,029 / ₹1,114 / ₹1,234 for FY27-29E, close to the street. The street values Bosch on **P/E on one-year-forward EPS** (MOSL ~40x FY28E). Applying the house rule (its clean forward P/E median since 2021, 33.6x, cut by the 9.4% auto-component de-rating) gives **30.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹1,174 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹32,654, DCF ₹26,836. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Momentum is strong, and regulation keeps adding content
arguments.p: Mobility grew 16.9% in FY26 and 25.7% in Q1FY27, well ahead of vehicle production (+11% and +22%), on gasoline and 2-wheeler engine management (OBD-II), premium motorcycles and a revived aftermarket. CAFE Phase 3 (Apr-2027, draft) and CV ADAS (Jan/Oct-2027) are the next content steps. But the GST 2.0 boost is a one-off step and the base turns tough from Q3FY27; management's own May outlook was "flattish".

arguments.h: RBIC is a good asset at a fair price, and it is now in the price
arguments.p: RBIC grew 17% a year in FY23-25 with a 19.3% EBITDA margin, against Bosch's 12.8%; it was bought at 10.6x EV/EBITDA, about a third of Bosch's own multiple. It adds ~19% to FY27E revenue and ~15% to FY27E EPS, because the ₹9,060 cr of cash it cost earned only ~6.5% before tax. The stock rose ~19% in three sessions after the announcement and ~30% since.

arguments.h: Much of the moat is rented from the parent
arguments.p: Royalty and technical fees (₹478 cr, +29%) and group professional and IT charges (₹1,097 cr, +24%) were 7.9% of FY26 revenue against an EBITDA margin of 13.2%; 58% of purchases come from group companies. That is why a dominant supplier earns 12-14% EBITDA margins, below Schaeffler, Sona or ZF CV. Exceptional gains from business sales (FY24, FY26) also flatter reported EPS history.

arguments.h: Valuation: the premium is not in the history
arguments.p: At ₹47,100 Bosch trades at 42.3x FY28E and 40.1x Sep-28E EPS, 29% above its own five-year trailing median, while the auto-component sector sits 9.4% below its medians. Its clean forward P/E has a median of 33.6x since Apr-2021; the market now pays ~40x for ~10-12% underlying EPS growth plus a one-time RBIC step. At the street's 40x our target would be ~₹46,960; the gap to the price is the multiple, not the earnings.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first quarter with RBIC consolidated (and restated comparatives), and the first full quarter on the smaller treasury.
Festive and post-festive production (Oct-2026 to Mar-2027) against the GST-boosted base of a year earlier.
Analyst visit to RBIC's Chakan plant (planned for November): RBIC's FY26 numbers, order book and capex.
Regulation: final CAFE Phase 3 norms (from Apr-2027), CV ADAS from Jan-2027, and any notification of ABS for all two-wheelers.
Joint ventures: merger-control approvals and first orders for the Tata AutoComp e-axle JV and the TSF air-systems JV; the FY27 dividend against the 55-85% policy.

sections.title: Robert Bosch's Indian flagship: engine management, aftermarket and power tools, and now braking and safety

blocks.p: Bosch Ltd (formerly MICO) is 70.54% owned by Robert Bosch GmbH and is the listed home of the group's mobility business in India. It reports three segments. **Automotive Products** (89% of FY26 revenue) combines three businesses whose revenue it does not split: **Power Solutions** (diesel and gasoline fuel injection, engine management and sensors for cars, trucks, tractors and off-highway machines), **2-Wheeler & Powersports** (engine management, sensors and ABS for motorcycles and scooters) and **Mobility Aftermarket** (spares, filters, spark plugs, wipers, batteries and lubricants sold through distributors and a workshop network). **Consumer Goods** (9%) is Bosch power tools, mostly bought from the group and resold. **Others** (2%) was building technology until it was sold in May-2025 and is now mainly rent and services. Sales outside India were 8.1% of revenue in FY26.

From Jul-2026 Bosch Ltd also owns 100% of **Bosch Chassis Systems India (RBIC)**, the group's Vehicle Motion business: ESP and ABS, braking actuation, airbag control units and vehicle-dynamics sensors, made at Chakan, Manesar and Sanand for Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors, Toyota, Bajaj Auto and others. It earned ₹3,936 cr of revenue in FY25 at a 19.3% EBITDA margin, against Bosch Ltd's 12.8%. Bosch paid ₹9,069 cr, almost all in cash. We include RBIC for the whole of FY27 (common-control accounting) at ~₹5,367 cr of revenue: about 19% of FY27E revenue and 25% of EBITDA.

sections.title: Seventy years of diesel, a BS-VI shock, a string of business sales and now a ₹9,069 cr purchase from the parent

blocks.p: Bosch Ltd grew up as the group's Indian maker of diesel fuel-injection pumps for trucks, tractors and gensets. Its last decade was shaped by the shift away from diesel: the BS-VI rules of Apr-2020 made small diesel cars uneconomic, revenue fell 19% in FY20 and the company booked ₹1,390 cr of restructuring charges in FY20-21. It then simplified: it sold its Project House mobility-solutions unit (FY24) and diagnostics (FY25) to group companies and building technologies (FY26) to Keenfinity, booking gains each time. In 2026 it reversed direction and bought RBIC from the parent. The pattern matters for valuation: reported EPS in FY20, FY21, FY24 and FY26 is not the run-rate.

sections.title: Vehicle production +11% in FY26 on GST 2.0; regulation keeps adding content, electrification threatens the oldest part

blocks.p: India produced 26.86 mn vehicles in FY26 (+11%), helped from Sep-2025 by GST 2.0, which cut the tax on small cars, two-wheelers up to 350cc, tractors and commercial vehicles. Passenger cars reached 5.61 mn (+10%). Q1FY27 production was 7.29 mn (+22%). Bosch is cautious beyond that: its own prognosis for FY27 was 26.86-28.27 mn ("flattish", May-2026), and it expects the market to grow only 3-4% a year to 2033. For a supplier the more important driver is content per vehicle, which regulation keeps raising.

bullets: **Electrification.** Bosch's own prognosis (May-2026): the overall Indian vehicle market grows 3-4% a year to 2033, with battery-electric penetration rising in buses, small (<2t) LCVs and cars on total cost of ownership. Power Solutions (fuel injection, engine management) is ICE content; RBIC's braking and safety content is powertrain-agnostic (EVs need new braking systems such as iBooster for regeneration). Bosch's e-axle entry is through a 50:50 JV with Tata AutoComp (first shipments Q3 of calendar 2027).

**Imports from the parent.** Bosch buys 58% of its inputs from related parties and traded goods are 40% of revenue; a weaker rupee or global price rises hit its gross margin (Q1FY27 −420bp) before it can pass them on. Localisation is management's answer ("well on track"), but the share bought from the parent rose to a decade high in FY26 (analyst on the Q1FY27 call).
**Aftermarket.** A large, fragmented market where Bosch competes with OE-branded parts and local brands; Bosch's growth was only 3.7% in FY26 before a new go-to-market push (+9.6% in Q1FY27).
**Power tools.** Cordless conversion and e-commerce; Bosch was first to get mandatory BIS certification for key tools (FY26), a barrier for cheap imports.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the tailwind is real and Bosch is one of its biggest beneficiaries by content, but it has turned into revenue more than into margin. Bosch's EBITDA margin rose only ~120bp from FY21 to FY26 while revenue doubled, because more of what it sells is designed and partly made by the parent and paid for through purchases, royalties and service fees. RBIC changes the mix (19% margin) but at a full price.

sections.title: Mobility: +17% in FY26 and +23% in Q1FY27, led by engine content; the aftermarket finally moving

blocks.p: Automotive Products earned ₹17,807 cr in FY26 (+14.5%) and a segment result of ₹2,557 cr (14.4% of revenue, after allocated depreciation). Power Solutions grew 17.6%, ahead of production (+11%): more gasoline injection and engine management in cars, plus trucks, tractors and off-highway machines. The 2-Wheeler business grew 69% on OBD-II sensors and engine management for premium motorcycles. The aftermarket grew only 3.7% as the independent aftermarket stagnated. In Q1FY27 the segment grew 25.7% (Power Solutions +29%, 2-Wheeler +41.4%, aftermarket +9.6%) with a 14.2% segment margin. Management called the Power Solutions gain "largely volume effect and maybe also some new introductions".

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we assume Automotive grows 15.5% in FY27 (Q2 +18%, Q3 +13%, Q4 +9% as the GST base bites), then 10% and 9%, with Bosch's own margin at 13.6% / 13.7% / 13.8%. That is above management's "flattish" May outlook and close to the run-rate since. The upside is CAFE 3 and CV ADAS content from 2027; the downside is that GST pulled demand forward and that every point of growth comes with more traded content from the parent.

sections.title: RBIC: the best business in the group's India portfolio, bought at a fair price from the parent

blocks.p: RBIC makes the brakes and safety electronics that regulation and buyers increasingly demand: ESP and ABS (it introduced both in India), conventional and new braking systems (iBooster and integrated power brakes for EVs), airbag control units and vehicle-dynamics sensors. Revenue grew from ₹2,887 cr (FY23) to ₹3,936 cr (FY25), 17% a year, and the EBITDA margin from 12.8% to 19.3% on localisation and a richer mix; 9MFY26 revenue was ₹3,533 cr. Management expects to "hold margins very steady for the next 5 years or so", with "some pressure" from OEM customisation, and says the order book is "very, very full". The portfolio is powertrain-agnostic: an electric car needs ESP and brakes as much as a petrol car.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** RBIC is the part of the Bosch story we like most: regulated, powertrain-agnostic content with a 19% margin. We model 13% / 12% / 11% growth (MOSL: 12% CAGR FY26-28E). The deal lifts our FY27E EPS by ~15% versus Bosch without RBIC (₹1029.0 vs ₹892.4), because the ₹9,060 cr it cost earned only ~6.5% before tax in the treasury. But the market priced this in: the stock rose ~19% in three sessions after the announcement and is up again since.

sections.title: Power tools: 9% of revenue, single-digit margins, a trading business

blocks.p: Consumer Goods (Bosch power tools) earned ₹1,836 cr in FY26 (+6.4%) and a segment result of ₹122 cr (6.6%), down from 11.4% in FY24. It is largely a trading business: Bosch bought ₹966 cr of goods from Robert Bosch Power Tools GmbH in FY26. Q1FY27 was strong (+20.9%, segment margin 10.9%) on construction demand and online sales. We grow it 12% / 10% / 10%; it matters little to value.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (annual reports, presentations and calls to Aug-2026, Screener.in peers)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Bosch has a real moat in India, built on the Bosch name, technology and OEM relationships, and RBIC adds the most defensible piece (safety systems). But the moat is largely rented from Robert Bosch GmbH: the listed company pays for technology (₹478 cr royalty), engineering and IT services (₹1,097 cr) and buys much of what it sells from the group. That is why a dominant supplier earns a 13% EBITDA margin. The moat protects revenue; the parent decides how much of the profit stays in India.

sections.title: Ten years to double revenue; margins never got back to the pre-BS-VI level

blocks.p: Bosch's revenue was ₹9,701 cr in FY16 and ₹20,035 cr in FY26: 7.5% a year. The decade had two halves. Up to FY19 Bosch earned an 18-19% EBITDA margin selling diesel fuel-injection systems; then the BS-VI emission rules (Apr-2020), Covid and the collapse of small diesel cars cut revenue by a fifth and the margin to 12% in FY21. Since then revenue has grown 15.6% a year (FY21-26) on vehicle volumes, gasoline and 2-wheeler engine management and the aftermarket, but the margin has only crept back from 12.0% to 13.2%. Reported EPS is noisy: restructuring charges cut it to ₹220 (FY20) and ₹163 (FY21); gains on selling businesses lifted it to ₹845 (FY24) and ₹940 (FY26). Before exceptional items EPS went from ₹330 (FY21) to ₹796 (FY26): ~19% a year.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the operating business has recovered but not re-rated its economics. Bosch Ltd sells much of what the group designs and partly makes elsewhere: 58% of its purchases are from related parties and traded goods are 40% of revenue, so its EBITDA margin sits well below listed peers such as Schaeffler or Sona. Until FY26 a ₹13,000-14,000 cr treasury added ₹800-850 cr a year of other income (28% of pre-tax profit before exceptional items). After the ₹9,060 cr cash payment for RBIC that cushion shrinks to ~₹400-450 cr; the earnings mix shifts from interest to operating profit, which is better quality but not more of it per share than the market already assumes.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Bosch does not give numerical guidance, and its May "flattish" outlook was overtaken within one quarter. The questions for the rest of FY27 are the GST base from Q3, the gross margin (more traded goods and a weaker rupee: ~₹96.6 to the dollar on 22-Jul-2026, MOSL daily), and how RBIC looks once consolidated. Our FY27E margin of {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} includes RBIC at ~19%; Bosch's own businesses at 13.6%, below Q1's 14.0%.

sections.title: An asset-light business that piled up cash, then spent two-thirds of it buying a sister company

blocks.p: Bosch needs little capital: net fixed assets were ₹1,654 cr at Mar-2026 against ₹20,035 cr of revenue, and cash capex has been only ₹300-650 cr a year. Over FY21-26 it generated ₹8,124 cr of operating cash, spent ₹2,268 cr on capex and paid ₹5,300 cr of dividends (₹1,023 cr of the FY26 cash dividend went to the parent). It also sold three businesses (Project House to a group company in FY24 for ₹781 cr, diagnostics to ETAS in FY25, building technologies to Keenfinity in FY26 for ₹595 cr). Returns were held down by the cash: ROCE of 14-22% since FY21 on Screener's basis. In Jul-2026 Bosch paid ₹9,060 cr in cash (plus 2,460 new shares) for RBIC; the new dividend policy (55-85% of profit) and RBIC's cash generation now decide how fast the treasury rebuilds.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** RBIC is the first big use of Bosch's cash in a decade, and it was bought from the parent. The price (10.6x FY25 EV/EBITDA, 16.6x FY25 profit) is reasonable next to Bosch's own ~35x EV/EBITDA, and minority shareholders approved it in a vote the promoter could not join. But the deal also means the parent converted a sister company into ~₹9,060 cr of cash, while Bosch Ltd swapped a ~6.5% pre-tax treasury yield for RBIC's ~8-9% after-tax earnings yield on the price. That is accretive (~15% to our FY27E EPS) and sensible; it is not a free lunch.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audit and good cash conversion, but one-offs and group charges cloud the history

bullets: **Cash conversion is good.** Cash from operations was 118% of net profit in FY25 and 78% in FY26 (2,175 cr); against profit before the ₹556 cr FY26 gain it was ~93%. Screener's CFO/EBITDA was 111-115% in FY25-26.

**One-offs are frequent.** Exceptional items moved reported profit materially in four of the last seven years: −₹645 cr (FY20), −₹745 cr (FY21), +₹844 cr (FY24), +₹556 cr (FY26). Gains came from selling businesses, twice to group companies. We value on EPS before exceptional items and forecast none.

**Treasury income was large and partly mark-to-market.** FY26 other income of ₹854 cr included ₹385 cr of gains on debt mutual funds, ₹296 cr of deposit interest and ₹112 cr of interest on loans to group companies. After the RBIC payment we forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} cr in FY27E and ₹{{F.otherIncome.1|num}} cr in FY28E (twelve months to Jun-26: ₹792 cr).

**Group charges grow faster than revenue.** Royalty and technical fees rose 29% to ₹478 cr (2.4% of revenue) and professional charges from group companies 24% to ₹1,097 cr (5.5%) in FY26, against revenue growth of 10.8%. These are expenses decided with the controlling shareholder.

**Lending to the group.** Bosch lends surplus cash to sister companies (₹950 cr at Mar-26, ₹1,370 cr a year earlier, secured and guaranteed by Robert Bosch GmbH, at 8.90-9.55%). It earns a fair rate, but it is a related-party exposure inside "treasury".
**The FY27 accounts will look different.** RBIC will be pooled (no goodwill) and FY26 restated; FY27 revenue growth of ~40% and a lower other-income line are accounting, not momentum.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Unqualified audit by S.R. Batliboi & Associates, no debt, good cash conversion. The amber is for frequent exceptional gains from business sales (some to group companies), the size and growth of royalties and group service fees, and the related-party lending; none is improper, but together they make reported EPS a poor guide and leave the minority dependent on the parent's transfer pricing.

sections.title: No debt; ₹13,600 cr of net treasury at Mar-26, ~₹5,600 cr after paying for RBIC

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Bosch held ₹6,783 cr of debt mutual funds and bonds, ₹4,271 cr of bank deposits, ₹950 cr of secured loans to Bosch group companies (8.90-9.55%, guaranteed by Robert Bosch GmbH), ₹396 cr of cash, ₹137 cr of accrued interest and ₹1,198 cr of listed and unlisted equity (HDFC Bank ₹892 cr, ICICI Bank ₹290 cr), against ₹119 cr of lease liabilities: ~₹13,600 cr net, ~₹4,600 a share. After the ₹9,060 cr RBIC payment (and RBIC's own ~₹1,030 cr of cash) the pro forma figure is ~₹5,640 cr, ~₹1,900 a share; the FY26 dividend (₹796 cr) was paid in Aug-2026. In our model the Mar-26 balance sheet is shown on this pro forma basis (investments and reserves both ₹8,020 cr lower), so the FY26 column of the balance sheet and FY26 ROE are not the reported ones (reported net worth ₹14,846 cr, ROE 19.4%). Working capital is light: inventory ~60 days, receivables ~50 days, payables ~98 days.

sections.title: Ownership: Robert Bosch 70.5%, Indian institutions 15%, foreign funds 7%

blocks.p: Robert Bosch GmbH owns 70.54% (Jun-2026) through Robert Bosch Internationale Beteiligungen AG (67.75%), Bosch Global Software Technologies (2.78%) and, since the RBIC deal, two tiny holdings (1,230 shares each). Nothing is pledged. Mutual funds own 6.67%, insurers 7.65% (GIC, New India and LIC together 5.9%), pension funds 0.67%, foreign portfolio investors 7.1% and resident individuals ~5.7%: the free float is under 30%, which keeps the stock thinly traded and index weights small.

blocks.callout: **Our read:** this is a subsidiary, not an owner-run company. The parent controls the board, the product roadmap, transfer prices and capital allocation, and it was on the other side of the largest deal in Bosch Ltd's history. Minority shareholders have protections (related-party votes, independent directors, a 55-85% payout policy) but not control.

sections.title: The street after Q1: Neutral to Reduce on valuation, targets ₹35,000-54,000

blocks.p: Coverage of Bosch is thin and mostly cautious. After the Q1FY27 results (10-Aug-2026) Motilal Oswal kept Neutral with ₹43,728 (~40x FY28E EPS of ₹1,093), calling the stock fairly valued at 44.6x/41.4x FY27E/FY28E; a Reduce-rated broker raised EPS 3-4% but kept ₹34,984, calling a 40-plus P/E rich for mid-teen growth; the highest target in coverage was ₹54,050 (Business Standard roundup, 31-Aug-2026, broker not visible to us). UBS had upgraded to Buy (₹45,530) in June on the RBIC deal and the JVs. Median of the three post-Q1 targets: ₹43,728, −7% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹47,100. Every house that shows its method uses **P/E on one-year-forward EPS**. The bulls focus on RBIC, regulation-led content and the margin recovery; the bears on valuation and on ICE exposure.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a quality franchise priced at 40x Sep-28E EPS; SELL

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** Robert Bosch's Indian mobility flagship: the leading supplier of engine management and fuel injection to Indian OEMs, a large aftermarket and power-tools business, and since Jul-2026 India's leading ESP/ABS and airbag-electronics maker (RBIC, 19% EBITDA margin). No debt, ~₹5,600 cr of treasury after the deal, a 55-85% payout policy and regulation (CAFE 3, CV ADAS, safety rules) adding content every year.

**What you are paying:** 45.8x our FY27E and 42.3x FY28E EPS for ~10-12% a year growth in Bosch's own businesses plus a one-time ~15% lift from RBIC. Since 2021 the market has paid a median 33.6x forward for Bosch on clean earnings, and auto-component stocks were 9.4% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026. On the street's own method and the house multiple the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): SELL. Even our bull case ({{scen.bull.tp|inr}}) is below the price.
